text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConserve hydrogen nuclei, solve the molecular fraction, and compare density-dependent chemical and gravitational clocks. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01The third atom carries away energy H + H + H → H₂ + H To form a bound molecule, two hydrogen atoms must transfer excess energy and momentum elsewhere. A third atom provides a collision partner that can carry them away. That partner remains an H atom after the event. This is a three-body chemical reaction, distinct from gravitational encounters involving three stars. This offers an entry to molecular formation in dense primordial gas with little dust. Supply a reaction coefficient and focus on how rapidly composition changes. The microscopic potential and quantum-scattering calculation belong in the reference, rather than becoming a separate subject in this guide. 02Count events separately from consumed atoms Define the event rate per volume and time by R₃ = k₃nH³. The adopted coefficient includes the counting convention; do not append an extra 1/3! factor. Each event makes one molecule and consumes two free atoms net. The third atom is present on both sides of the reaction. dnH₂dt=k₃nH³, dnHdt=−2k₃nH³ nN≡nH+2nH₂ = constant nN is the hydrogen-nucleus density, counting two nuclei inside each molecule. It remains constant in a closed, fixed-volume pure-hydrogen parcel. The sum of atom and molecule counts is not conserved: forming a molecule changes the number of independently moving particles. 03Solve for the fraction of nuclei in molecules x≡2nH₂nN, nH=nN(1−x) dxdt=2k₃nN²(1−x)³ Start with entirely atomic gas, x(0) = 0. Hold temperature and nucleus density fixed so k₃ is constant, then separate variables. Conversion slows as free atoms are depleted. A single initial rate therefore cannot be multiplied by an arbitrarily long time to obtain the final molecular fraction. ∫₀ˣdx′(1−x′)³=2k₃nN²t (1−x)−2−12=2k₃nN²t x=1−(1+4k₃nN²t)−1/2 x(t₅₀)=12 ⇒ t₅₀=34k₃nN² At x = 1/2, half the nuclei reside in molecules, but the molecular number density is nN/4, not nN/2. Keep the nuclei fraction and molecular particle count distinct when interpreting both the equations and the panel. 04Density changes the competition with gravity Use equation (6) of Forrey (2013) as the rate input. TK denotes the numerical temperature in kelvins; k₃ is in cm⁶ s⁻¹. The panel restricts temperature to 600–3000 K. This fit describes the specified reaction and does not replace an entire chemical network. TK≡T1 K, k₃=(6×10−32TK−1/4+2×10−31TK−1/2) cm⁶ s⁻¹ tff=√3π32GmₚnN t₅₀tff∝nN−3/2 (fixed T) Events scale as density cubed, while the rate per atom scales as density squared. This grows faster than the inverse free-fall time, which scales as nN¹ᐟ². High density can therefore make chemistry fast relative to gravity. The displayed tff is a uniform-sphere comparison clock; the chemical parcel itself is not collapsing. 05Molecular formation also affects thermal evolution Using about 4.48 eV for ground-state H₂ binding gives a binding-energy change of 4.48x/2 eV per initial nucleus. Its partition into heat, internal excitation, and later radiation requires additional physics. Since temperature is prescribed here, the panel reports only this energy scale and does not infer a temperature increase. A realistic primordial collapse couples reverse collisional dissociation, H₂ as a third partner, low-density H⁻ pathways, cooling, and compression. Reactions omitted here become especially consequential at high temperature and late conversion. The one-way model cannot determine chemical equilibrium or a self-consistent primordial-star trajectory. Relative to isothermal collapse, this is a small step that relaxes the assumption of fixed composition. A more complete model adds energy and fluid equations to the same nucleus bookkeeping. Identifying the conserved count and the competing clocks is a useful first step before solving that coupled system. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed temperature, increase hydrogen-nucleus density tenfold. How does the ratio of half-conversion time to free-fall time change? Show the answer and reasoning Since t₅₀ ∝ n⁻² and tff ∝ n⁻¹ᐟ², the ratio falls by 10⁻³ᐟ² ≈ 0.0316. Chemistry gains on the gravitational clock at high density; the chemical model itself holds temperature and density fixed.
